What can investors learn from Charlie Munger, Warren Buffett, and some of the greatest investors?

Here are 5 investing lessons worth remembering 👇 https://t.co/utyrnV3E5P

1️⃣ How to deal with market downturns

In 2009, Berkshire Hathaway was down 50%.

A reporter asked Charlie Munger whether he was worried.

His response offers a timeless lesson on investing through market crashes. https://t.co/c4WeFro3VV

5️⃣ Look for businesses with competitive advantages

Warren Buffett loves investing in (quasi-)monopolies.

Think Visa & Mastercard, S&P Global & Moody's, and Coca-Cola & PepsiCo.

These businesses benefit from powerful competitive advantages. https://t.co/UH8v4SmWL9

5. Microeconomics & Advantages of Scale

Munger emphasized "moats":

- Cost advantages (e.g., Walmart)
- Network effects (e.g., Coca-Cola’s distribution)
- Informational advantages (e.g., trusted brands)

Bigger often wins, but bureaucracy can kill giants too. https://t.co/pP7gSWoKjO

9. Berkshire's Secret:

Munger and Buffett didn’t make hundreds of decisions.

They made a few high-conviction bets, and loaded up when the odds were dramatically in their favor.

A few insights = extraordinary results. https://t.co/3V3PZC0aNZ

4. Some of the most expensive investing mistakes are the stocks you never bought.

Think Mastercard, Starbucks, and Constellation Software.

The calls from techbros and $NVDA stockbros to reinstate Jensen Huang illustrate a central theme of our time: the tension between national security and the private sector of an open society, when our principal adversary, CCP-ruled China, is not an open society and nationalizes whomever and whatever it wants within its borders (and sometimes outside too). A few decades ago, the U.S. government controlled dual-use technology superior to anything in the private sector. When commercial markets scaled, R&D spending skewed massively toward companies, and the government lost that dual-use edge.

It’s disingenuous to argue for Jensen’s return while casting his apparent ouster as punishment for banging subordinates. Office romances are the least of the problems here. Yes, America’s bloated legal industry has built a suboptimal liability structure around consensual office relationships, but a board can treat the occasional settlement as a cost of doing business. 

If Jensen intervened to ensure the supply of controlled GPUs to Megaspeed, that is far more serious. Yet, it still isn’t the worst issue.

Jensen’s true sin is that he advocated weakening export controls while sleeping with the adversary. Everybody talks their book (short sellers included). That kind of conflict is out in the open: you make more money if your view prevails. It is a far graver matter when a man with Jensen’s influence, over both whether controlled technology reached China and what the rules should be, has an undisclosed relationship that exposes him to romantic manipulation or blackmail. History is full of wreckage left by powerful men thinking with the other head.

Some argue that removing export controls on China makes us safer by keeping China dependent on us. That notion has been resoundingly disproven by decades of China stealing IP, forcing tech transfers, and then burying Western incumbents. When a smart, well-informed person argues for loose or no controls, it is almost always deliberate naiveté. If we value U.S. national security above shareholders' interest in seeing NVDA stock rebound, then Jensen must be held accountable by not regaining control of NVDA.
